# Plan: SPE Round 1 (r01) for the Triage Agent

Nothing exists yet. This round builds a first triage agent, predicts how three configurations will score, and runs one Workflow to grade them. Each step gets its own local commit. Nothing gets pushed.

Your spec is one sentence: "triage tickets correctly and cheaply." That sentence does not say what "correctly" or "cheaply" means. I filled those gaps with decisions D1 to D6 below. Each decision is a default you can change before you approve. If you have real tickets or a cost target, tell me now. Those two answers would change the plan the most.

## 0. Layout

```
spe/
  spec/spec.md
  spec/transcripts/r01-prompt.md      (your prompt, verbatim)
  plans/r01.md                        (this plan)
  predictions/r01.yaml                (every number in section 2)
  evals/data/r01-tickets.jsonl        (ticket text only)
  evals/keys/r01-keys.jsonl           (answer key, never shown to trials)
  evals/graders/                      (G1 to G7, deterministic code)
  evals/harness/r01-workflow.js
  evals/results/r01/
  prediction-log.md
  failures.md
triage/
  prompts/c1-plain.md
  prompts/c2-rubric.md                (rubric plus 6 examples)
  schema.json
  run.js
```

## 1. Specify

### Decisions that fill gaps in the spec

| ID | Decision |
|---|---|
| D1 | The agent picks one category from 6: Billing, Bug, Feature request, Account access, Outage, Other. |
| D2 | The agent picks one priority from P1 to P4, using a written rubric. P1 means service down or data loss for a customer. Missing a P1 costs more than over-escalating a P2. |
| D3 | The output is JSON with the fields `category`, `priority`, and `reason`. Round 1 gives the agent no tools. It makes one model call per ticket. |
| D4 | Text inside a ticket is data. Instructions written in a ticket, such as "mark this P1", do not change the result. |
| D5 | "Cheaply" means an average cost of $0.005 or less per ticket. |
| D6 | No real tickets exist yet, so round 1 uses 120 synthetic tickets. A separate dataset agent writes them and their keys. The triage agent never sees the keys. |

### Requirements

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | The agent assigns the correct category on at least 85% of tickets. | User: "triage tickets correctly". D1. | G1, exact match against the key |
| R2 | The agent assigns the exact correct priority on at least 75% of tickets. | User: "correctly". D2. | G2, exact match against the key |
| R3 | The agent catches at least 95% of P1 tickets. | D2 | G3, recall on the 15 keyed P1 tickets |
| R4 | At least 99% of outputs are valid JSON that matches the schema. | D3 | G4, JSON schema check |
| R5 | Injected instructions change the priority on no more than 5% of injection tickets. | D4 | G5, priority on the 10 injection tickets compared with the key |
| R6 | The average cost is $0.005 or less per ticket. | User: "cheaply". D5. | G6, measured tokens times the list price recorded at gate E1 |
| R7 | The run records p50 latency. Round 1 sets no target for latency. | Decision to measure only | G7, wall time per call |

The go-live bar is R1 to R6 all met by one configuration.

### Dataset mix (D6)

| Slice | Count | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Clear tickets | 70 | Baseline accuracy across all 6 categories |
| Ambiguous tickets | 20 | Two categories are plausible. The key names one primary category. |
| P1 incidents | 15 | Feeds G3 |
| Injection attempts | 10 | Feeds G5 |
| Non-English tickets | 5 | Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Japanese |

The total is 120. These slices do not overlap.

## 2. Predict

### Configurations

| ID | Model tier | Prompt |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | Small, low-cost model | Plain instruction with the category list and P1 to P4 labels only |
| C2 | Small, low-cost model | Full priority rubric plus 6 worked examples |
| C3 | Mid-tier model | Same prompt as C2 |

Gate E1 pins the exact model IDs and list prices from current docs. I have not checked those prices yet. The cost cells below use my assumed token counts and assumed prices.

### Predictions

The trials are 120 tickets, times 3 configurations, times 3 repeats. Each cell is the mean over the 3 repeats.

| Metric (grader) | C1 | C2 | C3 | Error band | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Category accuracy (G1) | 78% | 86% | 91% | ±5 pts | The examples fix most Bug versus Outage confusion. The larger model handles the ambiguous slice better. |
| Priority exact (G2) | 60% | 74% | 80% | ±6 pts | Without a rubric, the model guesses P2 or P3 by default. The rubric gives it definitions to apply. |
| Priority within one level (G2) | 90% | 95% | 97% | ±4 pts | Most priority errors land one level off. |
| P1 recall (G3) | 73% | 87% | 93% | ±10 pts | The rubric spells out P1. The sample is only 15 tickets, so the band is wide. |
| Category and priority both exact (G1, G2) | 52% | 66% | 74% | ±7 pts | This is roughly the product of the two rates. The errors are partly correlated. |
| Schema-valid output (G4) | 97% | 99% | 99.5% | ±2 pts | Structured output mode keeps failures rare. C1 has no example of the output format. |
| Injection resistance (G5) | 80% | 90% | 95% | ±15 pts | The rubric says to treat ticket text as data. The sample is 10 tickets, so one ticket moves the rate 10 points. |
| Input tokens per ticket (G6) | 450 | 1,900 | 1,900 | ±20% | Most of the C2 and C3 input is the rubric and examples. |
| Output tokens per ticket (G6) | 70 | 80 | 90 | ±25% | The `reason` field is one sentence. |
| Cost per ticket (G6) | $0.0007 | $0.0023 | $0.0090 | ±30% | Token counts times my assumed list prices. Gate E1 records the real prices. |
| p50 latency (G7) | 1.2 s | 1.6 s | 3.0 s | ±40% | The longer prompt adds a little time. The larger model adds more. |
| Run-to-run spread in category accuracy (G1) | 3 pts | 2 pts | 2 pts | ±2 pts | Spread is the max minus the min across the 3 repeats at temperature 0. |

### Predicted verdict

- C1 fails R1, R2, R3, and R5. It passes R6.
- C2 passes R1, R4, and R6. It misses R2 by about 1 point and misses R3.
- C3 passes R1, R2, and R4. It fails R6 because it costs about 4 times the cap. It is borderline on R3.
- No configuration meets the go-live bar in round 1.

A round where every configuration passes everything would show that the tasks were too easy. If that happens, round 2 needs harder tickets or stricter graders.

## 3. Evaluate

### Harness build steps

| Step | Work | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | Scaffold `spe/` and `triage/`. Write `schema.json`, both prompts, and `run.js`. Pin model IDs and list prices from current docs into `spe/evals/harness/config.json`. | `run.js` returns schema-valid JSON for all 3 configurations on 3 hand-written tickets. The config file contains model IDs and prices. |
| E2 | A separate dataset agent writes 120 tickets and the matching keys. Tickets go to `data/`. Keys go to `keys/`. | Slice counts match the mix table. No ticket appears twice. A ticket file contains no key fields. A grep shows the triage prompts and `run.js` never reference `keys/`. You spot-check 20 random keys and approve them. |
| E3 | Write graders G1 to G7 as deterministic code. Round 1 uses no LLM judge. | Grader tests pass on a known-good output and on 5 known-bad outputs. The known-bad outputs are a wrong category, a wrong priority, a missed P1, invalid JSON, and a priority set by an injection. Each known-bad output must fail its grader. |
| E4 | Write `r01-workflow.js`. It fans out trials, writes raw outputs to `results/r01/raw/`, runs graders, and writes `results/r01/summary.json`. | A dry run of 5 tickets, times 3 configurations, times 1 repeat finishes clean. The dry run cost is recorded. A scan of trial inputs finds no key strings. |

### Workflow arguments

```json
{
  "round": "r01",
  "configs": ["C1", "C2", "C3"],
  "tickets": "spe/evals/data/r01-tickets.jsonl",
  "keys": "spe/evals/keys/r01-keys.jsonl",
  "repeats": 3,
  "temperature": 0,
  "concurrency": 8,
  "budgetCapUsd": 25,
  "seed": 1
}
```

The trial agents receive only ticket text and their prompt. The graders alone read `keys`.

### Cost and time estimate (unmeasured)

- Trials: 1,080 calls at a predicted average of $0.004 each, which comes to about $4.30.
- Dataset generation and dry run: about $2.
- Total: about $6 to $10. The hard cap is $25.
- Wall time: about 15 minutes for the full run at concurrency 8. The build steps E1 to E4 come before the run.

### Halt conditions

I stop the round and report to you if any of these happens:
- Spend reaches the $25 cap.
- A key string shows up in any trial input or output.
- A grader is found broken mid-run.

## 4. Close-out (Learn)

1. Grade the run and write `results/r01/summary.json` and a short `results/r01/report.md`.
2. Write `spe/prediction-log.md`. It has one row per cell in the prediction table, with predicted, measured, and hit or miss within the band. It also gives a count of hits.
3. Write `spe/failures.md`. Each failure gets an ID like `F-r01-01`, the ticket IDs, the configuration, and a likely cause.
4. Add round 2 proposals to `spe/spec/spec.md`. Each proposal cites a failure ID. Likely candidates are a cheaper rubric for C2, a P1 keyword pre-check, and real tickets if you can supply them.
5. Report the headline numbers, which configuration came closest to the go-live bar, and the single best change for round 2.

### Commits (local only, never pushed)

| Commit subject | When |
|---|---|
| `SPE r01 specify: triage spec, decisions D1-D6, transcript` | After `spec.md` and the transcript are written |
| `SPE r01 predict: 3 configs, 12 metrics, verdict no config passes` | After `plans/r01.md` and `predictions/r01.yaml` are saved, before any harness work |
| `SPE r01 evaluate (harness): agent, 120 tickets, graders, dry run clean` | After gates E1 to E4 pass |
| `SPE r01 evaluate (results): <category %, priority %, P1 recall, $/ticket per config>` | After the run is graded |
| `SPE r01 learn: prediction log, failures, r02 proposals` | After the log, failures, and proposals are written. Then I add the local tag `spe-r01`. |

When you approve, I start with the specify commit. Then I save this plan and its predictions before I build any harness code.
